title: How Unix Spell Ran in 64kB RAM
excerpt: How do you fit a dictionary in 64kb RAM? Unix engineers solved it with clever data structures and compression tricks. Here's the fascinating story behind it.
content_html:
How do you fit a 250kB dictionary in 64kB of RAM and still perform fast lookups? For reference, even with modern compression techniques like gzip -9, you can't compress this file below 85kB.

In the 1970s, Douglas McIlroy faced this exact challenge while implementing the spell checker for Unix at AT&T. The constraints of the PDP-11 computer meant the entire dictionary needed to fit in just 64kB of RAM. A seemingly impossible task.

Instead of relying on generic compression techniques, he took advantage of the properties of the data and developed a compression algorithm that came within 0.03 bits of the theoretical limit of possible compression. To this day, it remains unbeaten.

The story of Unix spell is more than just historical curiosity. It's a masterclass in engineering under constraints: how to analyze a problem from first principles, leverage mathematical insights, and design elegant solutions that work within strict resource limits.

If you're short on time, here's the key engineering story:

  • The Unix spell started in the 1970s as an afternoon prototype by Steve Johnson at AT&T, before Douglas McIlroy rewrote it to improve its performance and accuracy.

  • McIlroy's first innovation was a clever linguistics-based stemming algorithm that reduced the dictionary to just 25,000 words while improving accuracy.

  • For fast lookups, he initially used a Bloom filter—perhaps one of its first production uses. Interestingly, Dennis Ritchie provided the implementation. They tuned it to have such a low false positive rate that they could skip actual dictionary lookups.

  • When the dictionary grew to 30,000 words, the Bloom filter approach became impractical, leading to innovative hash compression techniques.

  • They computed that 27-bit hash codes would keep collision probability acceptably low, but needed compression.

  • McIlroy's solution was to store differences between sorted hash codes, after discovering these differences followed a geometric distribution.

  • Using Golomb's code, a compression scheme designed for geometric distributions, he achieved 13.60 bits per word—remarkably close to the theoretical minimum of 13.57 bits.

  • Finally, he partitioned the compressed data to speed up lookups, trading a small memory increase (final size ~14 bits per word) for significantly faster performance.

The rest of the article expands each of these points and gives a detailed explanation with all the math and logic behind them.

In order to secure funding for Unix, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie pitched Unix as a text processing system for the patents department to AT&T. Naturally, a text processing system needed a spell checker as well.

The first version of Unix spell was written by Steve Johnson in 1975 which was a prototype. Jon Bentley mentions that Steve wrote it in one afternoon. Even though it worked, it was not very accurate.

It was pretty simple. It would split the input file into a stream of words, do some light preprocessing such as remove numbers and special characters, convert to lower case, then sort, unique, and finally pass the list to the spell program which would simply check for the existence of those words in a dictionary on the disk.

Because of its simplistic implementation, it was not very accurate, and also slow because of dictionary lookups on the disk.

After seeing the adoption of the initial version, Douglas McIlroy took up the project to rewrite it with the goal of improving the accuracy and performance of the tool. He worked on two separate fronts both involving some very clever engineering:

  • Building an affix removal algorithm for reducing words to their stems, and a compact dictionary consisting of the stem words

  • A compact data structure for loading the dictionary into memory for doing fast lookups

This article is going to be focused on the data structure design part, but let’s spend a section to get an overview on the affix removal algorithm to see how it worked.

Using a full fledged dictionary for doing lookups was slow because the computers those days had only a few kilobytes of main memory and using disk based lookups was even more slower.

Douglas McIlroy came up with the idea of an algorithm which would iteratively remove common prefixes and suffixes from a word and look up a dictionary to see if the reduced word is present in it or not. The algorithm would follow the affix removal process until there were no affixes left to remove and if even after this the word was not present in the dictionary, then it would be flagged as a misspelling.

For instance, the algorithm would reduce the word “misrepresented” to “present” by removing the prefixes “mis”, “re”, and the suffix “ed”. And because “present” is a valid word in the dictionary, it would not flag it as a misspelling.

This affix removal technique was not 100% accurate and would sometimes let misspelled words pass through. But, such occurrences were deemed acceptable at that time. He also implemented a bunch of exceptions to these rules to avoid some of the common errors.

Overall, this algorithm resulted in a very compact dictionary. The final dictionary consisted of 25,000 words, which seemed possible to load into memory with a well engineered data structure.

Let’s move on to discussing how he managed to implement in-memory dictionary lookups with just 64 kB of memory.

Bloom published his work on Bloom filter in 1970 while the Unix spell was developed in the mid-1970s. At this time, Bloom filter was not even called Bloom filter. In his paper, Douglas calls it a “superimposed code scheme”.

Interestingly, the Bloom filter implementation he used was given to him by Dennis Ritchie.

Even though the dictionary size was 25,000 words, it was still not possible to load it as it is in just 64kB of RAM. Besides, it also needed fast lookups.

The first data structure that Douglas used was a Bloom filter. In the paper he doesn’t call it Bloom filter, instead he refers to it as a “superimposed coding scheme”, attributed to Bloom’s paper from 1970. Interestingly, he gives the credit for the implementation of the Bloom filter he used to Dennis Ritchie.

A Bloom filter consists of a bit table initialized to all zeros. To add an item to the Bloom filter, you apply multiple hash functions to the item. Each hash function generates an index in the table, and that bit index is set to 1. If k hash functions are used, then, k different bit indices are turned on in the table.

For a more detailed explanation of Bloom filter, please check out my article on Bloom filters.

Looking up an item, whether it exists in the table or not, requires the same procedure. You need to apply the k hash functions, and for each of them check if the corresponding bit is set to 1 in the table or not. If even one of the bits is not on, then it means that the item is not present in the dataset. However, if all the bits are set, then it indicates that the item might be present, but this may also be a false positive.

False positives can occur because of hash collisions. When querying for an item, we cannot be 100% sure if a bit is on in the table because of the query item, or because of a hash collision with another item.

When using Bloom filter, you need to implement a strategy to handle false positives. For instance, in this case it could mean doing a full dictionary search. But that would defeat the whole purpose of using a Bloom filter, which was to save memory and do fast dictionary lookups. In the case of a spell checker, most of the words exist in the dictionary and only a fraction of words are misspelled, so we would be checking the full dictionary quite a lot.

However, a Bloom filter can be tuned to achieve a desired false positive rate. The following formula computes the false positive probability for a Bloom filter with a given size n, number of inserted items m, and number of hash functions k.

\(\begin{align*} &\text{q} \approx \left( 1 - e^{-\frac{kn}{m}} \right) \\ &\text{where:} & \\ &\text{q}:\ \text{Probability that a bit is 1} \\ &m: \ \text{Number of bits in the Bloom filter} \\ &k: \ \text{Number of hash functions used} \\ &n: \ \text{Number of elements inserted} \end{align*} \)

In his paper, Douglas mentions that a false positive probability of 1 in 2000 was acceptable to them, which meant that for such a low false positive rate, they did not need to consult the dictionary.

As they had a dictionary of 25,000 items, the number of items was fixed. They fixed the bit table size at 400,000 bits because of the limited amount of memory. Based on these factors, using 11 hash functions allowed them to keep the false positive rate at around 1/2000.

They used the Bloom filter based spell implementation for a while. In the paper, Douglas mentions that even though the false positive rate was acceptable, in the wild, they were encountering a lot of new words that needed to be added to the dictionary. This led to the dictionary size going up from 25,000 to 30,000.

However, for a dictionary of this size, their Bloom filter required a bigger bit table size which was not possible for them. As a result, Douglas looked for alternate data structure designs to be able to fit a dictionary of 30,000 words in memory with similar lookup performance and accuracy.

As the dictionary size exploded from 25,000 to 30,000, Douglas needed a more memory efficient data structure to hold the dictionary in memory.

A hash table was an attractive solution, but it would have consumed much more memory than a Bloom filter because it requires storing the hash, as well as, the actual words to handle collisions.

Instead of a full hash table, Douglas decided to store just the hashes of the words. The lookup required computing the hash of the input word, and then checking for its existence in the hashes using a scan.

One intuition for doing so might have been that the individual words can be of varying lengths, but a hash function will naturally compress them down to a fixed number of bits, and that may possibly allow them to fit the hashes in memory.

But hashes can collide, so they needed a large enough hash code to have an acceptably low probability of collisions.

If each word in the dictionary is hashed to a hash code of size b bits, then there are 2^b total possible hash codes in that space. If the size of the dictionary is v words, then the probability of a hash collision can be computed as:

\(\begin{align*} \text{P(hash collision)} = \frac{v}{2^b} \end{align*}\)

They had a dictionary of 30,000 words, which is ~2^15 words. Moreover, he mentions that a collision probability of 1 in 2^12 was acceptable to them. This gave a hash code size of 27 bits.

But 27-bit hash codes were too big: with 2^15 words, they needed 2^15 * 27 bits of memory, while the PDP-11 had only 2^15 * 16 bits (64kB) of RAM—compression was essential.

Before implementing any compression algorithm, we need to know what is the theoretical minimum number of bits we can achieve to compress this piece of data. It acts as a benchmark to tell us how well we are able to compress the data.

This theoretical minimum is computed using the information content of the event which generated the data we are trying to compress. This concept comes from information theory which is the underpinning foundation for all of the data compression techniques.

The basic idea behind information content is to use the probability of an event to determine how many bits are needed to encode it without loss of information.

A highly likely event carries less information (for instance a 100% probable event has no information and needs 0 bits to encode), while a less probable event contains much more information and needs more bits. There is an inverse relationship between the probability of an event and its information content, which leads to the following formula:

\(\begin{align*} &\text{I(E)} = \log_2\left(\frac{1}{P(E)}\right) \\ &\text{Or, I(E) = } -\log_2{P(E)} \\ &\text{where P(E) is } \text{probability of event E} \end{align*}\)

Now, to compute the information content of a set of hash codes, we need to figure out the probability of generating them.

If the size of a hash code is b bits, then there are a total of 2^b possible hash codes in that space. Out of that, we are selecting a set of v unique hash codes.

\( \begin{align*} \text{The total number of ways to select such sets = }\binom{2^b}{v} \end{align*} \)

Therefore, the probability of any one of these sets of being generated is:

\(\begin{align*} \text{P} = \frac{1}{\binom{2^b}{v}} \end{align*} \)

Thus, the information content of these hash codes is:

\(\begin{align*} &I(E) = - \log_2\left(\frac{1}{\binom{2^b}{v}}\right) \\ &= \log_2\left(\binom{2^b}{v}\right) \\ &= \log_2\left(\frac{(2^b)!}{v! \, (2^b - v)!}\right) \end{align*}\)

To simplify things, we can use Stirling’s approximation:

\(\begin{align*} &\text{Stirling's approximation: } \quad \log_2(n!) \approx n \log_2(n) - n \log_2(e), \\ \end{align*} \)

The paper makes another simplifying assumption that the number of words in the dictionary (30,000) is much smaller than the total number of hash codes (2^27), i.e., v « 2^b, this allows them to simplify (2^b - v) as 2^b in the above computation.

Using these two approximations leads to the following formula for the information content:

\(\begin{align*} &I(E) \approx v\left[b - \log_2\left(\frac{v}{e}\right)\right] \end{align*}\)

Plugging in v=30,000 and b=27, the minimum number of bits needed to encode a single hash code turns out to be 13.57, which was ~50% shorter than the original hash codes, and within the capacity of the PDP-11’s memory.

At this point they knew how much compression they could achieve but the bigger question was how to get there. Instead of compressing the raw hash codes, what if they computed and stored the differences between successive hash codes (in their sorted order)? This is similar to how delta encoding works, but not quite the same.

There were a couple of advantages of working with hash differences.

  • By definition the differences were smaller than the raw hash codes

  • And many of the difference value would repeat because the difference of several hash codes might be the same.

This implied that it was easier to compress these differences than the hash codes.

Hash differences were computed by sorting the hash codes and taking differences between consecutive values.

To check if a word exists in the dictionary or not, they would compute the hash of the word and check for its existence in the dictionary via a simple algorithm.

Now, let’s discuss how they came up with a compression scheme for this data.

The basic principle behind lossless compression is to assign shorter codes to symbols with higher probabilities, and longer codes to symbols with lower probabilities. This makes sense because symbols with higher probabilities tend to occur more frequently in the data and assigning them shorter codes means higher compression rate.

But this requires computing the probability distribution of all the symbols in the data, and then using it to generate compressed codes. The probability distribution table is needed at decompression time as well to perform the decoding.

This had two problems for Douglas:

  • Holding a probability distribution table for ~30,000 symbols in memory would have taken away any compression advantage he was getting from compression itself. So he needed a scheme which was free of this requirement.

  • Computing the probabilities of the hash differences would have been time expensive. All the 30,000 possible hash difference values, their sums and counts would not have been possible to keep in memory for computing their probabilities. So, it would have required an expensive disk based data structure to compute these probabilities.

But McIlroy came up with an elegant solution by recognizing that the hash differences followed a geometric distribution, enabling an efficient compression scheme. Let’s first understand how these hash difference values are geometrically distributed.

The geometric distribution is a discrete probability distribution which is used to model scenarios where we conduct an experiment until we get a success. For instance, rolling a six-faced die until we get a “1” forms a geometric distribution, with the probability of success being 1/6. A simpler example is tossing a coin until we get a head.

If the probability of failure is p, the probability of success is q, and if success occurs in the kth trial, then the probability mass function of the geometric distribution is given by the following formula:

\(\begin{align*} &P = p^kq \end{align*}\)

Now, let's understand how the hash difference values map to this distribution.

As each hash code is b bits wide, we have a space of 2^b points. And we have v hash codes spread out in this space. The probability of any point in this space containing a hash code is q=v/2^b, and the probability of a point being empty is p=1-(v/2^b).

\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(a point containing a hash code)} = q = \frac{v}{2^b} \\ &\text{P(an empty point)} = p = 1 - \left(\frac{v}{2^b}\right) \end{align*}\)

But we are interested in modelling the distribution of hash difference values, rather than the hash codes themselves. A hash difference k occurs when two consecutive hash values in the sorted sequence are k positions apart. For instance, if we have two successive hash code values 20 and 25, then the hash difference is 5.

What's the probability of seeing a hash difference of k? Given any hash value h in our space:

  • We need the next k-1 positions after h to be empty

  • And then we need a hash value at position h+k

  • The probability of k-1 empty positions is p^(k-1)

  • The probability of a hash value at position h+k is q

Therefore, the probability of a hash difference of k is:

\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(difference=k) =} p^\left(k-1\right)q \end{align*}\)

This follows exactly the form of a geometric distribution!

If you read the spell paper, you will find that the author takes a different route to arrive at this conclusion. He models the generation of the hash codes as a Poisson process and proceeds from there.

But, what is the point of modelling this as a geometric distribution? It turns out, there is a very simple and efficient run-length encoding scheme for geometrically distributed integers given by Golomb in his 1965 paper. Let’s see how it works.

Golomb’s code is a simple run-length encoding scheme for geometrically distributed integers which was used by Douglas to compress the hash differences. It takes advantage of the fact that geometrically distributed values have an exponentially decaying probability of success, which can be leveraged for performing compression.

What do we mean by that? Recall that in the case of geometric distribution, the probability of success after k trials is given as:

\(P = p^kq\)

Let’s say, we find an integer m, such that p^m = 1/2. Then, it means that the probability of success after k + m trials is:

\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(success after k + m trials)} = p^\left(k + m\right)q = \frac{1}{2}p^kq \end{align*}\)

In other words, the probability of getting success in k + m trials is half of that of the probability of getting a success in k trials. And this probability continues to half every m successive trials. This is an exponentially decaying distribution of probabilities.

Let's consider a fair coin toss example where we toss the coin until a head occurs. For a fair coin, p = q = 1/2.

Here, we have m = 1, because p^1 = 1/2. It means that the probabilities decay by half every trial:

\(\begin{align*} &P(k=1) = \frac{1}{2} \\ &P(k=2) = \frac{1}{4} \\ &P(k=3) = \frac{1}{8} \\ &P(k=4) = \frac{1}{16} \end{align*}\)

Let’s take another example of a biased coin, such that p=1/sqrt(2) = 0.707, and q=0.293.

Here, we have m=2, because p^2 = 1/2. In this case the probabilities decay after blocks of size 2.

\(\begin{align*} &P(k=1) = 0.293 \\ &P(k=2) = 0.207 \\ &P(k=3) = 0.116 \\ &P(k=4) = 0.104 \\ &P(k=5) = 0.073 \\ &P(k=6) = 0.051 \end{align*}\)

You can see that the probabilities decay by half for every even value of k. For instance:

\(\frac{P(k=2)}{P(k=4)} = \frac{P(K=4)}{P(k=6)} \approx 0.5\)

This pattern of exponential decay allows us to group the hash difference values in blocks of size m. Each value within a block gets a code of size k bits, while the next block gets codes of size k + 1 bits. The reasoning behind it is rooted in information theory.

The minimum number of bits required to encode the outcome of an event is given by its information content which is -log₂(p), where p is the probability of that event.

It means that if an event has probability 1/2, it needs 1 bit code, an event with probability 1/4 needs 2 bits, an event with probability 1/8 needs 3 bit codes and so on.

We can leverage this for geometrically distributed values by arranging them in blocks of size m. The values within a given block can be assigned codes of equal length, and the values in the subsequent block gets codes one bit wider for its m values.

It turns out, formation of blocks with increasingly larger codes also leads to a beautiful self-similar bit pattern with properties that make it very easy to generate such codes. Let’s see how this self-similar pattern forms.

Self-similar pattern essentially means that the codes at a specific index within a block repeats itself at the same index in the next block, with one padding bit added on its left.

For instance, if the code at the 2nd position in the first block is 0001, then the 2nd code in the 2nd block will be 10001. Similarly, the 2nd position code in the 3rd block will be 110001, and so on.

This self-similar pattern naturally emerges because of the enforcement of 1 bit longer codes in each successive block. Let us see a concrete example.

Let’s say, our block size is m=5 and the codes in the first block are k=4 bits wide.

If the first code in the first block is 0110, then we can generate the codes for the rest of the block by adding 1 to the previous code value. The codes for the first block will look like this:

As you can see, the first block ends at the code 1010. The natural value for the next code should be 1011, but because this code lies in the next block, its code has to be 1 bit larger. As a result we need to left shift it by one bit, which makes it 10110. And if you notice the least 4 bits of this code are the same as the first code in the first block. The following diagram highlights this visually.

Another thing worth noticing here is that we are obtaining the first value of the 2nd block by left shifting it by 1 bit, which means its least significant bit (LSB) is always 0.
For the self-similar patterns to form, the first code of the first block should also always have its LSB set to 0. This implies that this first code is always an even number of the form 2x.

The self-similar code has a couple of additional properties which provide an intuitive way to figure out the minimum bit width k for the codes in the first block. Let’s see how.

To figure out the minimum number of bits needed to encode the first block, let’s assume the first encoded value in the first block is 2x.

Then the first code of the 2nd block should be 2x + m. However, because the codes in the next block need to be 1 bit wider, this value gets shifted to the left by 1 bit, which makes it 2(2x + m).

Left shifting a value by 1 bit doubles it.

The self-similarity pattern gives rise to another way to think about these codes. If the first code in the first block is 2x, then in the next block:

  • We want the same pattern (2x)

  • But with an extra bit on the left

  • Adding a bit on the left is equivalent to adding 2^k

  • So the code becomes 2^k + 2x

Combining these two relations gives us the following equation

\(\begin{align*} &2^k + 2x = 2(2x + m) \\ &\text{Or, } 2^k = 2m + 2x \\ &\text{Here, x is a nonnegative integer, so we can simplify the above to:} \\ &2^k \ge 2m \end{align*}\)

By solving for the smallest integer value of k we can get the code width of the first block.

The same equation also gives us the value of x:

\(\begin{align*} x = 2^{(k-1)} - m = 2^{\lceil \log_2 m \rceil} - m \end{align*} \)

Knowing the values of m, k, and x gives way for a simple encoding algorithm.

The paper by Golomb gave a different algorithm for encoding and decoding, but the Unix spell code used a slightly complicated but more efficient algorithm. I describe the algorithm as implemented in the Unix spell.

Let’s understand how to encode a value using Golomb’s code. Recall that we have:

  • Initial bit width k

  • Block size m

  • First code in first block is 2x, where x = 2^(k-1) - m

The decoding process is also not that complicated. Given a code, we need to:

  1. First look at its top k-1 bits (call this w):

    • If w is less than x, then this is a shorter code

    • The decoded value is simply w itself

  2. If w ≥ x, then we need to

    • Include one more bit into w

    • Look at the least significant k bits of w: call it u

    • if u < 2x + m:

      • value = x + u + (s - 1)m

      • where s is the number of extra bits included into w

    • else:

      • keep including more bits into w until u < 2x + m

You can find the original Unix svr4 implementation of the decode algorithm here.

So how well this technique was able to compress the hash differences?

Recall that the theoretical limit of compression was 13.57 bits per word. Golomb codes managed to achieve an expected code length of 13.60, remarkably close to this theoretical minimum.

However, looking up a value in this compressed dictionary was quite slow. It required starting from the beginning, decoding and summing values until finding or exceeding the desired hash code.

To speed this up, the final Unix spell implementation partitioned the table of differences into M bins. This allowed them to first locate the correct bin, and then only scan within that bin, speeding up the search by a factor of M.

This partitioning scheme required storing additional pointers to the bins, adding log₂M bits per word to the storage requirement. The total storage increased to about 14 bits per word, but this was an acceptable trade-off: it was still within their memory budget while providing significantly faster lookups.

Share

The Unix spell command is a fascinating piece of engineering history that emerged from the severe memory constraints of the PDP-11. What makes it particularly interesting is how it evolved from a simple disk-based dictionary lookup to an elegant solution combining multiple computer science concepts:

  • Probabilistic data structures (Bloom filters)

  • Information theory (optimal bit width calculations)

  • Probability theory (geometric distribution)

  • Compression algorithms (Golomb coding)

The engineering journey is particularly instructive:

  1. Started with Bloom filters achieving acceptable false positive rates

  2. When dictionary size grew, switched to compressed hashing where:

    • They computed theoretical minimum bits needed

    • Recognized patterns in hash differences

    • Used Golomb's code to achieve near-optimal compression

    • Added binning for faster lookups with minimal space overhead

Even though modern spell checkers use different techniques like edit distance and language models, the engineering insights from Unix spell remain valuable. It shows how deep understanding of theoretical concepts combined with practical constraints can lead to efficient and elegant solutions.

Most importantly, it demonstrates that some of the best innovations happen when we are resource constrained, forcing us to think deeper about our problems rather than throwing more hardware at them.

But, such occurrences were deemed acceptable at that time. He also implemented a bunch of exceptions to these rules to avoid some of the common errors. Overall, this algorithm resulted in a very compact dictionary. The final dictionary consisted of 25,000 words, which seemed possible to load into memory with a well engineered data structure.Let’s move on to discussing how he managed to implement in-memory dictionary lookups with just 64 kB of memory.Bloom published his work on Bloom filter in 1970 while the Unix spell was developed in the mid-1970s. At this time, Bloom filter was not even called Bloom filter. In his paper, Douglas calls it a “superimposed code scheme”. Interestingly, the Bloom filter implementation he used was given to him by Dennis Ritchie.Even though the dictionary size was 25,000 words, it was still not possible to load it as it is in just 64kB of RAM. Besides, it also needed fast lookups. The first data structure that Douglas used was a Bloom filter. In the paper he doesn’t call it Bloom filter, instead he refers to it as a “superimposed coding scheme”, attributed to Bloom’s paper from 1970. Interestingly, he gives the credit for the implementation of the Bloom filter he used to Dennis Ritchie.A Bloom filter consists of a bit table initialized to all zeros. To add an item to the Bloom filter, you apply multiple hash functions to the item. Each hash function generates an index in the table, and that bit index is set to 1. If k hash functions are used, then, k different bit indices are turned on in the table.For a more detailed explanation of Bloom filter, please check out my article on Bloom filters.Looking up an item, whether it exists in the table or not, requires the same procedure. You need to apply the k hash functions, and for each of them check if the corresponding bit is set to 1 in the table or not. If even one of the bits is not on, then it means that the item is not present in the dataset. However, if all the bits are set, then it indicates that the item might be present, but this may also be a false positive. False positives can occur because of hash collisions. When querying for an item, we cannot be 100% sure if a bit is on in the table because of the query item, or because of a hash collision with another item. When using Bloom filter, you need to implement a strategy to handle false positives. For instance, in this case it could mean doing a full dictionary search. But that would defeat the whole purpose of using a Bloom filter, which was to save memory and do fast dictionary lookups. In the case of a spell checker, most of the words exist in the dictionary and only a fraction of words are misspelled, so we would be checking the full dictionary quite a lot.However, a Bloom filter can be tuned to achieve a desired false positive rate. The following formula computes the false positive probability for a Bloom filter with a given size n, number of inserted items m, and number of hash functions k. \(\begin{align*} &\text{q} \approx \left( 1 - e^{-\frac{kn}{m}} \right) \\ &\text{where:} & \\ &\text{q}:\ \text{Probability that a bit is 1} \\ &m: \ \text{Number of bits in the Bloom filter} \\ &k: \ \text{Number of hash functions used} \\ &n: \ \text{Number of elements inserted} \end{align*} \)In his paper, Douglas mentions that a false positive probability of 1 in 2000 was acceptable to them, which meant that for such a low false positive rate, they did not need to consult the dictionary. As they had a dictionary of 25,000 items, the number of items was fixed. They fixed the bit table size at 400,000 bits because of the limited amount of memory. Based on these factors, using 11 hash functions allowed them to keep the false positive rate at around 1/2000.They used the Bloom filter based spell implementation for a while. In the paper, Douglas mentions that even though the false positive rate was acceptable, in the wild, they were encountering a lot of new words that needed to be added to the dictionary. This led to the dictionary size going up from 25,000 to 30,000.However, for a dictionary of this size, their Bloom filter required a bigger bit table size which was not possible for them. As a result, Douglas looked for alternate data structure designs to be able to fit a dictionary of 30,000 words in memory with similar lookup performance and accuracy.As the dictionary size exploded from 25,000 to 30,000, Douglas needed a more memory efficient data structure to hold the dictionary in memory. A hash table was an attractive solution, but it would have consumed much more memory than a Bloom filter because it requires storing the hash, as well as, the actual words to handle collisions.Instead of a full hash table, Douglas decided to store just the hashes of the words. The lookup required computing the hash of the input word, and then checking for its existence in the hashes using a scan. One intuition for doing so might have been that the individual words can be of varying lengths, but a hash function will naturally compress them down to a fixed number of bits, and that may possibly allow them to fit the hashes in memory.But hashes can collide, so they needed a large enough hash code to have an acceptably low probability of collisions.If each word in the dictionary is hashed to a hash code of size b bits, then there are 2^b total possible hash codes in that space. If the size of the dictionary is v words, then the probability of a hash collision can be computed as:\(\begin{align*} \text{P(hash collision)} = \frac{v}{2^b} \end{align*}\)They had a dictionary of 30,000 words, which is ~2^15 words. Moreover, he mentions that a collision probability of 1 in 2^12 was acceptable to them. This gave a hash code size of 27 bits.But 27-bit hash codes were too big: with 2^15 words, they needed 2^15 * 27 bits of memory, while the PDP-11 had only 2^15 * 16 bits (64kB) of RAM—compression was essential. Before implementing any compression algorithm, we need to know what is the theoretical minimum number of bits we can achieve to compress this piece of data. It acts as a benchmark to tell us how well we are able to compress the data.This theoretical minimum is computed using the information content of the event which generated the data we are trying to compress. This concept comes from information theory which is the underpinning foundation for all of the data compression techniques. The basic idea behind information content is to use the probability of an event to determine how many bits are needed to encode it without loss of information. A highly likely event carries less information (for instance a 100% probable event has no information and needs 0 bits to encode), while a less probable event contains much more information and needs more bits. There is an inverse relationship between the probability of an event and its information content, which leads to the following formula:\(\begin{align*} &\text{I(E)} = \log_2\left(\frac{1}{P(E)}\right) \\ &\text{Or, I(E) = } -\log_2{P(E)} \\ &\text{where P(E) is } \text{probability of event E} \end{align*}\)Now, to compute the information content of a set of hash codes, we need to figure out the probability of generating them.If the size of a hash code is b bits, then there are a total of 2^b possible hash codes in that space. Out of that, we are selecting a set of v unique hash codes. \( \begin{align*} \text{The total number of ways to select such sets = }\binom{2^b}{v} \end{align*} \)Therefore, the probability of any one of these sets of being generated is:\(\begin{align*} \text{P} = \frac{1}{\binom{2^b}{v}} \end{align*} \)Thus, the information content of these hash codes is:\(\begin{align*} &I(E) = - \log_2\left(\frac{1}{\binom{2^b}{v}}\right) \\ &= \log_2\left(\binom{2^b}{v}\right) \\ &= \log_2\left(\frac{(2^b)!}{v! \, (2^b - v)!}\right) \end{align*}\)To simplify things, we can use Stirling’s approximation:\(\begin{align*} &\text{Stirling's approximation: } \quad \log_2(n!) \approx n \log_2(n) - n \log_2(e), \\ \end{align*} \)The paper makes another simplifying assumption that the number of words in the dictionary (30,000) is much smaller than the total number of hash codes (2^27), i.e., v « 2^b, this allows them to simplify (2^b - v) as 2^b in the above computation. Using these two approximations leads to the following formula for the information content:\(\begin{align*} &I(E) \approx v\left[b - \log_2\left(\frac{v}{e}\right)\right] \end{align*}\)Plugging in v=30,000 and b=27, the minimum number of bits needed to encode a single hash code turns out to be 13.57, which was ~50% shorter than the original hash codes, and within the capacity of the PDP-11’s memory.At this point they knew how much compression they could achieve but the bigger question was how to get there. Instead of compressing the raw hash codes, what if they computed and stored the differences between successive hash codes (in their sorted order)? This is similar to how delta encoding works, but not quite the same.There were a couple of advantages of working with hash differences.By definition the differences were smaller than the raw hash codesAnd many of the difference value would repeat because the difference of several hash codes might be the same. This implied that it was easier to compress these differences than the hash codes. Hash differences were computed by sorting the hash codes and taking differences between consecutive values.For instance:Let’s also see how the lookup of a word worked when they stored hash differences instead of the actual value.To check if a word exists in the dictionary or not, they would compute the hash of the word and check for its existence in the dictionary via a simple algorithm. Now, let’s discuss how they came up with a compression scheme for this data.The basic principle behind lossless compression is to assign shorter codes to symbols with higher probabilities, and longer codes to symbols with lower probabilities. This makes sense because symbols with higher probabilities tend to occur more frequently in the data and assigning them shorter codes means higher compression rate.But this requires computing the probability distribution of all the symbols in the data, and then using it to generate compressed codes. The probability distribution table is needed at decompression time as well to perform the decoding. This had two problems for Douglas:Holding a probability distribution table for ~30,000 symbols in memory would have taken away any compression advantage he was getting from compression itself. So he needed a scheme which was free of this requirement.Computing the probabilities of the hash differences would have been time expensive. All the 30,000 possible hash difference values, their sums and counts would not have been possible to keep in memory for computing their probabilities. So, it would have required an expensive disk based data structure to compute these probabilities.But McIlroy came up with an elegant solution by recognizing that the hash differences followed a geometric distribution, enabling an efficient compression scheme. Let’s first understand how these hash difference values are geometrically distributed.The geometric distribution is a discrete probability distribution which is used to model scenarios where we conduct an experiment until we get a success. For instance, rolling a six-faced die until we get a “1” forms a geometric distribution, with the probability of success being 1/6. A simpler example is tossing a coin until we get a head. If the probability of failure is p, the probability of success is q, and if success occurs in the kth trial, then the probability mass function of the geometric distribution is given by the following formula:\(\begin{align*} &P = p^kq \end{align*}\)Now, let's understand how the hash difference values map to this distribution.As each hash code is b bits wide, we have a space of 2^b points. And we have v hash codes spread out in this space. The probability of any point in this space containing a hash code is q=v/2^b, and the probability of a point being empty is p=1-(v/2^b).\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(a point containing a hash code)} = q = \frac{v}{2^b} \\ &\text{P(an empty point)} = p = 1 - \left(\frac{v}{2^b}\right) \end{align*}\)But we are interested in modelling the distribution of hash difference values, rather than the hash codes themselves. A hash difference k occurs when two consecutive hash values in the sorted sequence are k positions apart. For instance, if we have two successive hash code values 20 and 25, then the hash difference is 5.What's the probability of seeing a hash difference of k? Given any hash value h in our space:We need the next k-1 positions after h to be emptyAnd then we need a hash value at position h+kThe probability of k-1 empty positions is p^(k-1)The probability of a hash value at position h+k is qTherefore, the probability of a hash difference of k is:\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(difference=k) =} p^\left(k-1\right)q \end{align*}\)This follows exactly the form of a geometric distribution!If you read the spell paper, you will find that the author takes a different route to arrive at this conclusion. He models the generation of the hash codes as a Poisson process and proceeds from there.But, what is the point of modelling this as a geometric distribution? It turns out, there is a very simple and efficient run-length encoding scheme for geometrically distributed integers given by Golomb in his 1965 paper. Let’s see how it works.Golomb’s code is a simple run-length encoding scheme for geometrically distributed integers which was used by Douglas to compress the hash differences. It takes advantage of the fact that geometrically distributed values have an exponentially decaying probability of success, which can be leveraged for performing compression.What do we mean by that? Recall that in the case of geometric distribution, the probability of success after k trials is given as:\(P = p^kq\)Let’s say, we find an integer m, such that p^m = 1/2. Then, it means that the probability of success after k + m trials is:\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(success after k + m trials)} = p^\left(k + m\right)q = \frac{1}{2}p^kq \end{align*}\)In other words, the probability of getting success in k + m trials is half of that of the probability of getting a success in k trials. And this probability continues to half every m successive trials. This is an exponentially decaying distribution of probabilities.Let's consider a fair coin toss example where we toss the coin until a head occurs. For a fair coin, p = q = 1/2.Here, we have m = 1, because p^1 = 1/2. It means that the probabilities decay by half every trial:\(\begin{align*} &P(k=1) = \frac{1}{2} \\ &P(k=2) = \frac{1}{4} \\ &P(k=3) = \frac{1}{8} \\ &P(k=4) = \frac{1}{16} \end{align*}\)Let’s take another example of a biased coin, such that p=1/sqrt(2) = 0.707, and q=0.293.Here, we have m=2, because p^2 = 1/2. In this case the probabilities decay after blocks of size 2.\(\begin{align*} &P(k=1) = 0.293 \\ &P(k=2) = 0.207 \\ &P(k=3) = 0.116 \\ &P(k=4) = 0.104 \\ &P(k=5) = 0.073 \\ &P(k=6) = 0.051 \end{align*}\)You can see that the probabilities decay by half for every even value of k. For instance:\(\frac{P(k=2)}{P(k=4)} = \frac{P(K=4)}{P(k=6)} \approx 0.5\)This pattern of exponential decay allows us to group the hash difference values in blocks of size m. Each value within a block gets a code of size k bits, while the next block gets codes of size k + 1 bits. The reasoning behind it is rooted in information theory.The minimum number of bits required to encode the outcome of an event is given by its information content which is -log₂(p), where p is the probability of that event. It means that if an event has probability 1/2, it needs 1 bit code, an event with probability 1/4 needs 2 bits, an event with probability 1/8 needs 3 bit codes and so on.We can leverage this for geometrically distributed values by arranging them in blocks of size m. The values within a given block can be assigned codes of equal length, and the values in the subsequent block gets codes one bit wider for its m values.Arranging hash code differences in blocks of sizes m, where each block’s probability is half of that of its predecessor. If the predecessor block gets k bit wide codes, the next block gets k+1 bit wide codes.It turns out, formation of blocks with increasingly larger codes also leads to a beautiful self-similar bit pattern with properties that make it very easy to generate such codes. Let’s see how this self-similar pattern forms.Self-similar pattern essentially means that the codes at a specific index within a block repeats itself at the same index in the next block, with one padding bit added on its left.For instance, if the code at the 2nd position in the first block is 0001, then the 2nd code in the 2nd block will be 10001. Similarly, the 2nd position code in the 3rd block will be 110001, and so on. This self-similar pattern naturally emerges because of the enforcement of 1 bit longer codes in each successive block. Let us see a concrete example.Let’s say, our block size is m=5 and the codes in the first block are k=4 bits wide. If the first code in the first block is 0110, then we can generate the codes for the rest of the block by adding 1 to the previous code value. The codes for the first block will look like this:As you can see, the first block ends at the code 1010. The natural value for the next code should be 1011, but because this code lies in the next block, its code has to be 1 bit larger. As a result we need to left shift it by one bit, which makes it 10110. And if you notice the least 4 bits of this code are the same as the first code in the first block. The following diagram highlights this visually.An example of self-similar codes. The first code in the first block are same as least 4 bits of the first code in the 2nd block Another thing worth noticing here is that we are obtaining the first value of the 2nd block by left shifting it by 1 bit, which means its least significant bit (LSB) is always 0. For the self-similar patterns to form, the first code of the first block should also always have its LSB set to 0. This implies that this first code is always an even number of the form 2x.The self-similar code has a couple of additional properties which provide an intuitive way to figure out the minimum bit width k for the codes in the first block. Let’s see how.To figure out the minimum number of bits needed to encode the first block, let’s assume the first encoded value in the first block is 2x. Then the first code of the 2nd block should be 2x + m. However, because the codes in the next block need to be 1 bit wider, this value gets shifted to the left by 1 bit, which makes it 2(2x + m).Left shifting a value by 1 bit doubles it.The self-similarity pattern gives rise to another way to think about these codes. If the first code in the first block is 2x, then in the next block:We want the same pattern (2x)But with an extra bit on the leftAdding a bit on the left is equivalent to adding 2^kSo the code becomes 2^k + 2xCombining these two relations gives us the following equation\(\begin{align*} &2^k + 2x = 2(2x + m) \\ &\text{Or, } 2^k = 2m + 2x \\ &\text{Here, x is a nonnegative integer, so we can simplify the above to:} \\ &2^k \ge 2m \end{align*}\)By solving for the smallest integer value of k we can get the code width of the first block.The same equation also gives us the value of x:\(\begin{align*} x = 2^{(k-1)} - m = 2^{\lceil \log_2 m \rceil} - m \end{align*} \)Knowing the values of m, k, and x gives way for a simple encoding algorithm.The paper by Golomb gave a different algorithm for encoding and decoding, but the Unix spell code used a slightly complicated but more efficient algorithm. I describe the algorithm as implemented in the Unix spell.Let’s understand how to encode a value using Golomb’s code. Recall that we have:Initial bit width kBlock size mFirst code in first block is 2x, where x = 2^(k-1) - mHere’s the encoding algorithm:The following figure shows two examples to illustrate how it works in practice:Examples of how the encoding algorithm works for values 2 and 8You can find the original Unix svr4 implementation of this algorithm here.The decoding process is also not that complicated. Given a code, we need to:First look at its top k-1 bits (call this w):If w is less than x, then this is a shorter codeThe decoded value is simply w itselfIf w ≥ x, then we need to Include one more bit into wLook at the least significant k bits of w: call it uif u < 2x + m:value = x + u + (s - 1)mwhere s is the number of extra bits included into welse:keep including more bits into w until u < 2x + mYou can find the original Unix svr4 implementation of the decode algorithm here.So how well this technique was able to compress the hash differences?Recall that the theoretical limit of compression was 13.57 bits per word. Golomb codes managed to achieve an expected code length of 13.60, remarkably close to this theoretical minimum.However, looking up a value in this compressed dictionary was quite slow. It required starting from the beginning, decoding and summing values until finding or exceeding the desired hash code.To speed this up, the final Unix spell implementation partitioned the table of differences into M bins. This allowed them to first locate the correct bin, and then only scan within that bin, speeding up the search by a factor of M.This partitioning scheme required storing additional pointers to the bins, adding log₂M bits per word to the storage requirement. The total storage increased to about 14 bits per word, but this was an acceptable trade-off: it was still within their memory budget while providing significantly faster lookups.ShareThe Unix spell command is a fascinating piece of engineering history that emerged from the severe memory constraints of the PDP-11. What makes it particularly interesting is how it evolved from a simple disk-based dictionary lookup to an elegant solution combining multiple computer science concepts:Probabilistic data structures (Bloom filters)Information theory (optimal bit width calculations)Probability theory (geometric distribution)Compression algorithms (Golomb coding)The engineering journey is particularly instructive:Started with Bloom filters achieving acceptable false positive ratesWhen dictionary size grew, switched to compressed hashing where:They computed theoretical minimum bits neededRecognized patterns in hash differencesUsed Golomb's code to achieve near-optimal compressionAdded binning for faster lookups with minimal space overheadEven though modern spell checkers use different techniques like edit distance and language models, the engineering insights from Unix spell remain valuable. It shows how deep understanding of theoretical concepts combined with practical constraints can lead to efficient and elegant solutions.Most importantly, it demonstrates that some of the best innovations happen when we are resource constrained, forcing us to think deeper about our problems rather than throwing more hardware at them.Development of a Spelling List by Douglas McIlroy, 1982Run-length Encodings by Golomb, 1965Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors by Bloom, 1970A Spelling Checker by Jon Bentley, 1985History of UnixGeometric DistributionBloom filterUnix Spell Source If you find my work interesting and valuable, you can support me by opting for a paid subscription (it’s $6.40 monthly/$58 annual). You need to apply the k hash functions, and for each of them check if the corresponding bit is set to 1 in the table or not. If even one of the bits is not on, then it means that the item is not present in the dataset. However, if all the bits are set, then it indicates that the item might be present, but this may also be a false positive.

如何将 250kB 的字典放入 64kB RAM 中并仍然执行快速查找？ 作为参考，即使使用 gzip -9 等现代压缩技术，也无法将此文件压缩到 85kB 以下。

20 世纪 70 年代，Douglas McIlroy 在 AT&T 实施 Unix 拼写检查器时面临着这一挑战。 PDP-11 计算机的限制意味着整个字典只需 64kB RAM 即可容纳。 看似不可能完成的任务。

他没有依赖通用压缩技术，而是利用数据的特性，开发了一种压缩算法，该算法与可能压缩的理论极限相差不到 0.03 位。 直到今天，它仍然保持不败。

Unix 咒语的故事不仅仅是历史好奇心。 这是限制下的工程大师班：如何从第一原理分析问题，利用数学见解，并设计在严格的资源限制内工作的优雅解决方案。

如果您时间有限，以下是关键的工程故事：

  • Unix 咒语始于 20 世纪 70 年代，当时 AT&T 的史蒂夫·约翰逊 (Steve Johnson) 在下午制作了一个原型，之后道格拉斯·麦克罗伊 (Douglas McIlroy) 重写了它以提高其性能和准确性。
  • McIlroy 的第一个创新是一种基于语言学的巧妙的词干算法，该算法将词典减少到只有 25,000 个单词，同时提高了准确性。
  • 为了快速查找，他最初使用了布隆过滤器——这可能是其最初的生产用途之一。 有趣的是，丹尼斯·里奇（Dennis Ritchie）提供了实现。 他们将其调整为具有如此低的误报率，以至于他们可以跳过实际的字典查找。
  • 当字典增长到 30,000 个单词时，布隆过滤器方法变得不切实际，从而催生了创新的哈希压缩技术。
  • 他们计算出 27 位哈希码可以将冲突概率保持在可接受的低水平，但需要压缩。
  • 麦克罗伊的解决方案是存储排序哈希码之间的差异，发现这些差异遵循几何分布。
  • 使用 Golomb 代码（一种为几何分布设计的压缩方案），他实现了每个字 13.60 位，非常接近理论最小值 13.57 位。
  • 最后，他对压缩数据进行分区以加快查找速度，以少量内存增加（最终大小约为每字 14 位）换取显着更快的性能。

本文的其余部分扩展了每一点，并对其背后的所有数学和逻辑进行了详细解释。

为了确保 Unix 的资金，Ken Thompson 和 Dennis Ritchie 向 AT&T 推荐 Unix 作为专利部门的文本处理系统。 当然，文本处理系统也需要拼写检查器。

Unix拼写的第一个版本是由Steve Johnson于1975年编写的，它是一个原型。 乔恩·本特利提到史蒂夫在一个下午写下了这本书。 尽管它有效，但不是很准确。

这很简单。 它将输入文件分割成单词流，进行一些简单的预处理，例如删除数字和特殊字符，转换为小写，然后排序，唯一，最后将列表传递给拼写程序，该程序将简单地检查磁盘上的字典中是否存在这些单词。

由于它的实现过于简单，所以它不是很准确，而且由于在磁盘上进行字典查找，速度也很慢。

在看到初始版本被采用后，Douglas McIlroy 开始重写该项目，目标是提高该工具的准确性和性能。 他在两个不同的领域工作，都涉及一些非常聪明的工程：

  • 构建词缀删除算法，将单词减少到词干，以及由词干组成的紧凑词典
  • 紧凑的数据结构，用于将字典加载到内存中以进行快速查找

本文将重点讨论数据结构设计部分，但让我们花一部分时间来概述词缀删除算法，看看它是如何工作的。

使用成熟的字典进行查找速度很慢，因为当时的计算机只有几千字节的主内存，并且使用基于磁盘的查找速度更慢。

道格拉斯·麦克罗伊提出了一种算法的想法，该算法可以迭代地从单词中删除常见的前缀和后缀，并查找字典以查看减少的单词是否存在于其中。 该算法将遵循词缀删除过程，直到没有词缀需要删除为止，如果即使在此之后该单词不存在于词典中，那么它也会被标记为拼写错误。

例如，该算法通过删除前缀“mis”、“re”和后缀“ed”，将“misrepresented”一词减少为“present”。 而且因为“present”在字典中是一个有效的单词，所以它不会将其标记为拼写错误。

这种词缀去除技术并不是 100% 准确，有时会漏掉拼写错误的单词。 但是，这种情况在当时被认为是可以接受的。 他还对这些规则实施了一系列例外，以避免一些常见错误。

总的来说，该算法产生了一个非常紧凑的字典。 最终的词典由 25,000 个单词组成，看起来可以通过精心设计的数据结构加载到内存中。

让我们继续讨论他如何仅用 64 kB 内存实现内存中字典查找。

Bloom 于 1970 年发表了有关 Bloom filter 的著作，而 Unix 咒语则是在 20 世纪 70 年代中期开发的。 此时，布隆过滤器甚至不被称为布隆过滤器。 道格拉斯在他的论文中将其称为“叠加代码方案”。

有趣的是，他使用的布隆过滤器实现是 Dennis Ritchie 给他的。

尽管词典大小为 25,000 个单词，但仍然无法加载，因为它的 RAM 仅有 64kB。 此外，它还需要快速查找。

道格拉斯使用的第一个数据结构是布隆过滤器。 在论文中，他没有将其称为布隆过滤器，而是将其称为“叠加编码方案”，源自 Bloom 1970 年的论文。 有趣的是，他将自己使用的布隆过滤器的实现归功于 Dennis Ritchie。

布隆过滤器由初始化为全零的位表组成。 要将项目添加到布隆过滤器，您可以对该项目应用多个哈希函数。 每个哈希函数都会在表中生成一个索引，并且该位索引设置为 1。 如果使用k个散列函数，则在表中打开k个不同的位索引。

关于布隆过滤器更详细的解释，请查看我关于布隆过滤器的文章。

查找某个项目，无论它是否存在于表中，都需要相同的过程。 您需要应用 k 个哈希函数，并为每个函数检查表中相应位是否设置为 1。 如果其中一位未打开，则意味着该项目不存在于数据集中。 然而，如果所有位均已设置，则表明该项目可能存在，但这也可能是误报。

由于哈希冲突，可能会出现误报。 查询某个项目时，我们无法 100% 确定表中某个位是否因查询项目或与另一个项目的哈希冲突而打开。

使用布隆过滤器时，您需要实施一种策略来处理误报。 例如，在这种情况下，这可能意味着进行完整的字典搜索。 但这将违背使用布隆过滤器的全部目的，即节省内存并进行快速字典查找。 就拼写检查器而言，大多数单词都存在于字典中，只有一小部分单词拼写错误，因此我们需要大量检查完整的字典。

然而，可以调整布隆过滤器以达到所需的误报率。 以下公式计算具有给定大小 n、插入项数 m 和哈希函数数 k 的布隆过滤器的误报概率。

\(\begin{align*} &\text{q} \approx \left( 1 - e^{-\frac{kn}{m}} \right) \\ &\text{where:} & \\ &\text{q}:\ \text{一位为 1 的概率} \\ &m: \ \text{布隆过滤器中的位数} \\ &k: \ \text{使用的哈希函数数量} \\ &n: \ \text{数字插入的元素数量} \end{align*} \)

道格拉斯在论文中提到，2000 年有 1 分之一的误报概率对他们来说是可以接受的，这意味着对于如此低的误报率，他们不需要查阅字典。

由于他们的字典有 25,000 个项目，因此项目数量是固定的。 由于内存量有限，他们将位表大小固定为 400,000 位。 基于这些因素，使用 11 个哈希函数使他们能够将误报率保持在 1/2000 左右。

他们使用基于布隆过滤器的拼写实现有一段时间了。 道格拉斯在论文中提到，尽管误报率是可以接受的，但在野外，他们遇到了大量需要添加到词典中的新单词。 这导致字典大小从 25,000 增加到 30,000。

然而，对于这种大小的字典，他们的布隆过滤器需要更大的位表大小，这对他们来说是不可能的。 因此，Douglas 寻找替代数据结构设计，以便能够在内存中容纳 30,000 个单词的字典，同时具有相似的查找性能和准确性。

随着字典大小从 25,000 激增至 30,000，Douglas 需要一种内存效率更高的数据结构来将字典保存在内存中。

哈希表是一个有吸引力的解决方案，但它会比布隆过滤器消耗更多的内存，因为它需要存储哈希以及处理冲突的实际单词。

道格拉斯决定只存储单词的哈希值，而不是完整的哈希表。 查找需要计算输入单词的哈希值，然后使用扫描检查哈希值中是否存在该单词。

这样做的一种直觉可能是各个单词可以具有不同的长度，但哈希函数会自然地将它们压缩到固定数量的位，这可能允许它们适合内存中的哈希值。

但哈希值可能会发生冲突，因此它们需要足够大的哈希码才能具有可接受的低冲突概率。

如果字典中的每个单词都被哈希为大小为 b 位的哈希码，则该空间中总共有 2^b 个可能的哈希码。 如果字典的大小是 v 个单词，则哈希冲突的概率可以计算为：

\(\begin{align*} \text{P(哈希冲突)} = \frac{v}{2^b} \end{align*}\)

他们有一本包含 30,000 个单词的字典，大约是 2^15 个单词。 此外，他提到 2^12 中 1 的碰撞概率对他们来说是可以接受的。 这给出了 27 位的哈希码大小。

但 27 位哈希码太大：对于 2^15 个字，它们需要 2^15 * 27 位内存，而 PDP-11 只有 2^15 * 16 位 (64kB) RAM - 压缩至关重要。

在实现任何压缩算法之前，我们需要知道理论上可以压缩该数据块的最小位数是多少。 它充当基准，告诉我们压缩数据的能力如何。

该理论最小值是使用生成我们尝试压缩的数据的事件的信息内容来计算的。 这个概念来自信息论，它是所有数据压缩技术的基础。

信息内容背后的基本思想是使用事件的概率来确定需要多少位来对其进行编码而不丢失信息。

可能性较高的事件携带较少的信息（例如，100% 可能性的事件没有信息，需要 0 位进行编码），而可能性较小的事件则包含更多信息，需要更多位。 事件的概率与其信息内容之间存在反比关系，从而得出以下公式：

\(\begin{align*} &\text{I(E)} = \log_2\left(\frac{1}{P(E)}\right) \\ &\text{或者，I(E) = } -\log_2{P(E)} \\ &\text{其中 P(E) 是 } \text{事件 E 的概率} \end{align*}\)

现在，为了计算一组哈希码的信息内容，我们需要计算出生成它们的概率。

如果哈希码的大小为 b 位，则该空间中总共有 2^b 种可能的哈希码。 其中，我们选择一组 v 个唯一的哈希码。

\( \begin{align*} \text{选择此类集合的方式总数 = }\binom{2^b}{v} \end{align*} \)

因此，生成这些集合中任意一组的概率为：

\(\begin{align*} \text{P} = \frac{1}{\binom{2^b}{v}} \end{align*} \)

因此，这些哈希码的信息内容为：

\(\begin{align*} &I(E) = - \log_2\left(\frac{1}{\binom{2^b}{v}}\right) \\ &= \log_2\left(\binom{2^b}{v}\right) \\ &= \log_2\left(\frac{(2^b)!}{v! \, (2^b - v)!}\right) \end{align*}\)

为了简化事情，我们可以使用斯特林近似：

\(\begin{align*} &\text{斯特林近似: } \quad \log_2(n!) \approx n \log_2(n) - n \log_2(e), \\ \end{align*} \)

论文做了另一个简化假设，字典中的单词数量（30,000）远小于哈希码总数（2^27），即 v « 2^b，这使得他们可以在上述计算中将（2^b - v）简化为 2^b。

使用这两个近似值可得出以下信息内容公式：

\(\begin{align*} &I(E) \approx v\left[b - \log_2\left(\frac{v}{e}\right)\right] \end{align*}\)

代入 v=30,000 和 b=27，编码单个哈希码所需的最小位数为 13.57，比原始哈希码短约 50%，并且在 PDP-11 内存的容量范围内。

此时，他们知道可以实现多少压缩，但更大的问题是如何实现这一目标。 如果他们不压缩原始哈希码，而是计算并存储连续哈希码之间的差异（按排序顺序）会怎样？ 这与增量编码的工作原理类似，但并不完全相同。

使用哈希差异有几个优点。

  • 根据定义，差异小于原始哈希码
  • 并且许多差异值会重复，因为几个哈希码的差异可能相同。

这意味着压缩这些差异比哈希码更容易。

哈希差异是通过对哈希代码进行排序并获取连续值之间的差异来计算的。

例如：

我们还可以看看当它们存储哈希差异而不是实际值时，单词的查找是如何工作的。

为了检查字典中是否存在某个单词，他们将计算该单词的哈希值，并通过简单的算法检查它是否存在于字典中。

现在，我们来讨论一下他们是如何为这些数据想出一个压缩方案的。

无损压缩背后的基本原理是将较短的代码分配给具有较高概率的符号，并将较长的代码分配给具有较低概率的符号。 这是有道理的，因为具有较高概率的符号往往在数据中更频繁地出现，并且为它们分配较短的代码意味着更高的压缩率。

但这需要计算数据中所有符号的概率分布，然后用它来生成压缩代码。 解压缩时也需要概率分布表来执行解码。

这给道格拉斯带来了两个问题：

  • 在内存中保留约 30,000 个符号的概率分布表会剥夺他从压缩本身获得的任何压缩优势。 所以他需要一个没有这个要求的方案。
  • 计算哈希差异的概率会花费大量时间。 所有 30,000 个可能的哈希差值、它们的总和和计数不可能保存在内存中以计算它们的概率。 因此，需要昂贵的基于磁盘的数据结构来计算这些概率。

但麦克罗伊认识到哈希差异遵循几何分布，从而提出了一个优雅的解决方案，从而实现了高效的压缩方案。 我们先来了解一下这些哈希差值是如何几何分布的。

几何分布是一种离散概率分布，用于对我们进行实验直至成功的场景进行建模。 例如，滚动六面骰子直到得到“1”，形成几何分布，成功的概率为 1/6。 一个更简单的例子是抛硬币，直到出现正面。

如果失败的概率为 p，成功的概率为 q，如果第 k 次试验成功，则几何分布的概率质量函数由以下公式给出：

\(\begin{align*} &P = p^kq \end{align*}\)

现在，让我们了解哈希差值如何映射到该分布。

由于每个哈希码都是 b 位宽，因此我们有 2^b 个点的空间。 我们有 v 个散列码分布在这个空间中。 该空间中任意点包含哈希码的概率为 q=v/2^b，点为空的概率为 p=1-(v/2^b)。

\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(包含哈希码的点)} = q = \frac{v}{2^b} \\ &\text{P(空点)} = p = 1 - \left(\frac{v}{2^b}\right) \end{align*}\)

但我们感兴趣的是对哈希差值的分布建模，而不是哈希码本身。 当排序序列中两个连续的哈希值相距 k 个位置时，就会出现哈希差异 k。 例如，如果我们有两个连续的哈希码值 20 和 25，则哈希差为 5。

看到 k 的哈希差异的概率是多少？ 给定我们空间中的任何哈希值 h：

  • 我们需要 h 之后的接下来的 k-1 个位置为空
  • 然后我们需要一个h+k位置的哈希值
  • k-1 个空位置的概率为 p^(k-1)
  • 位置 h+k 处的哈希值的概率为 q

因此，k的哈希差值的概率为：

\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(difference=k) =} p^\left(k-1\right)q \end{align*}\)

这完全遵循几何分布的形式！

如果你读过拼写论文，你会发现作者采取了不同的途径得出这个结论。 他将哈希码的生成建模为泊松过程，并从那里开始。

但是，将其建模为几何分布有什么意义呢？ 事实证明，Golomb 在他 1965 年的论文中给出了一种非常简单且有效的几何分布整数游程编码方案。 让我们看看它是如何工作的。

哥伦布代码是一种简单的几何分布整数游程编码方案，道格拉斯使用它来压缩哈希差异。 它利用了几何分布值具有指数衰减成功概率的事实，可用于执行压缩。

我们这么说是什么意思？ 回想一下，在几何分布的情况下，k 次试验后的成功概率如下：

\(P = p^kq\)

假设我们找到一个整数 m，使得 p^m = 1/2。 那么，这意味着经过 k + m 次尝试后成功的概率为：

\(\begin{align*} &\text{P(k + m 次试验后成功)} = p^\left(k + m\right)q = \frac{1}{2}p^kq \end{align*}\)

换句话说，k + m 次试验成功的概率是 k 次试验成功概率的一半。 并且这个概率每 m 次连续试验就会减半。 这是概率的指数衰减分布。

让我们考虑一个公平的抛硬币例子，我们抛硬币直到出现正面。 对于公平的硬币，p = q = 1/2。

这里，我们有 m = 1，因为 p^1 = 1/2。 这意味着每次试验的概率都会衰减一半：

\(\begin{align*} &P(k=1) = \frac{1}{2} \\ &P(k=2) = \frac{1}{4} \\ &P(k=3) = \frac{1}{8} \\ &P(k=4) = \frac{1}{16} \end{align*}\)

我们再举一个有偏差硬币的例子，p=1/sqrt(2) = 0.707，q=0.293。

这里，我们有 m=2，因为 p^2 = 1/2。 在这种情况下，概率在大小为 2 的块之后衰减。

\(\begin{align*} &P(k=1) = 0.293 \\ &P(k=2) = 0.207 \\ &P(k=3) = 0.116 \\ &P(k=4) = 0.104 \\ &P(k=5) = 0.073 \\ &P(k=6) = 0.051 \end{align*}\)

您可以看到，对于 k 的每个偶数值，概率都会衰减一半。 例如：

\(\frac{P(k=2)}{P(k=4)} = \frac{P(K=4)}{P(k=6)} \约0.5\)

这种指数衰减模式允许我们将散列差值分组到大小为 m 的块中。 块内的每个值都获得大小为 k 位的代码，而下一个块则获得大小为 k + 1 位的代码。 其背后的推理植根于信息论。

对事件结果进行编码所需的最小位数由其信息内容给出，即 -log2(p)，其中 p 是该事件的概率。

这意味着如果事件的概率为1/2，则需要1位代码，概率为1/4的事件需要2位代码，概率为1/8的事件需要3位代码，依此类推。

我们可以通过将几何分布值排列成大小为 m 的块来利用它。 给定块内的值可以被分配相同长度的代码，并且后续块中的值获得比其m个值宽一位的代码。

事实证明，用越来越大的代码形成的块也会产生美丽的自相似位模式，其属性使得生成此类代码变得非常容易。 让我们看看这种自相似模式是如何形成的。

自相似模式本质上意味着块内特定索引处的代码在下一个块中的相同索引处重复，并在其左侧添加一个填充位。

例如，如果第一个块中第二个位置的代码是 0001，那么第二个块中的第二个代码将为 10001。 同样，第 3 个块中的第 2 个位置代码将为 110001，依此类推。

\(\begin{align*} &2^k + 2x = 2(2x + m) \\ &\text{或者, } 2^k = 2m + 2x \\ &\text{这里，x是非负整数，所以我们可以将上面简化为：} \\ &2^k \ge 2m \end{align*}\)

通过求解 k 的最小整数值，我们可以得到第一个块的码宽。

那么这种技术压缩哈希差异的效果如何呢？

回想一下，压缩的理论极限是每字 13.57 位。 Golomb 代码成功实现了 13.60 的预期代码长度，非常接近这一理论最小值。

然而，在这个压缩字典中查找值非常慢。 它需要从头开始，对值进行解码和求和，直到找到或超过所需的哈希码。

为了加快速度，最终的 Unix 拼写实现将差异表划分为 M 个容器。 这使得他们能够首先找到正确的 bin，然后只在该 bin 内进行扫描，从而将搜索速度提高了 M 倍。

这种分区方案需要存储指向 bin 的附加指针，从而为每个字增加了 log2M 位的存储要求。 总存储增加到每个字约 14 位，但这是一个可以接受的权衡：它仍在内存预算之内，同时提供了更快的查找速度。
